    DHI MIKE DFSU results with pyramids-mesh¶

    DFSU is DHI's flexible-mesh format for MIKE 21/3 hydrodynamic results. It stores an unstructured mesh (mixed triangles and quads) with time-varying variables such as surface elevation and depth-averaged velocity. pyramids-mesh reads it through mikeio under the hood and presents a standard MeshDataset.

    Setup¶

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset

# Paths are relative to THIS notebook (docs/examples/), never the repo root.
# read_file takes a pathlib.Path - pass Path objects, never str().
DATA = Path("../../examples/data")
DATA.resolve()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles
    from pathlib import Path import numpy as np from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset # Paths are relative to THIS notebook (docs/examples/), never the repo root. # read_file takes a pathlib.Path - pass Path objects, never str(). DATA = Path("../../examples/data") DATA.resolve() import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles

    Quickstart read¶

    Pass driver="dfsu". This is the classic MIKE OdenseHD2D estuary example - 535 nodes, 724 faces.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(DATA / "dhi" / "OdenseHD2D.dfsu", driver="dfsu")
ds
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(DATA / "dhi" / "OdenseHD2D.dfsu", driver="dfsu") ds
    Out[3]:
    MeshDataset(mesh='mesh2d', n_node=535, n_face=724, n_edge=0, variables=['Surface elevation', 'Depth averaged U velocity', 'Depth averaged V velocity', 'node_z'])
    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    from cleopatra.config import Config
Config.set_matplotlib_backend()
    from cleopatra.config import Config Config.set_matplotlib_backend()
    Out[4]:
    'inline'

    The variables are Surface elevation and the two depth-averaged velocity components (Depth averaged U/V velocity), plus the static bed level node_z.

    Explore the dataset¶

    A MeshDataset wraps a UGRID-style unstructured mesh plus any data variables that ride on it. The scalar properties below describe the grid at a glance: how many nodes and faces it has, its coordinate reference system, and its spatial extent.

    The coordinates are a projected UTM grid (metres), even though no CRS is embedded.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    print("n_node:", ds.n_node)
print("n_face:", ds.n_face)
print("crs:   ", ds.crs)
print("epsg:  ", ds.epsg)
print("bounds:", ds.bounds)  # (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)
    print("n_node:", ds.n_node) print("n_face:", ds.n_face) print("crs: ", ds.crs) print("epsg: ", ds.epsg) print("bounds:", ds.bounds) # (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)
    n_node: 535
n_face: 724
crs:    None
epsg:   None
bounds: (211068.5, 6153077.5, 224171.625, 6164499.5)

    crs/epsg are often None: many hydraulic-model result files store coordinates without an embedded CRS, so pyramids reports the geometry faithfully and leaves georeferencing to you. The bounds tuple is the mesh envelope in the file's own coordinate units.

    Data variables¶

    data_variable_names lists every field attached to the mesh. These are the real model results - water levels, depths, velocities - that make a results file worth reading.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    ds.data_variable_names
    ds.data_variable_names
    Out[6]:
    ['Surface elevation',
 'Depth averaged U velocity',
 'Depth averaged V velocity',
 'node_z']

    summary() returns a tidy pandas.DataFrame of per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std) - a quick sanity check on magnitudes and fill values.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    ds.summary()
    ds.summary()
    Out[7]:
    count min max mean std
    variable
    Surface elevation 9395 -0.247714 0.444137 0.143018 0.179092
    Depth averaged U velocity 9395 -0.322162 0.307246 0.013443 0.051201
    Depth averaged V velocity 9395 -0.634840 1.071846 0.012656 0.057671
    node_z 535 -11.131345 -0.200000 -3.595227 2.870370

    The Mesh2d geometry¶

    ds.mesh is a Mesh2d: the topology the data variables are defined on. Nodes carry the (x, y) coordinates; face_node_connectivity says which nodes form each face (a row per face, padded to the maximum vertex count).

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    mesh = ds.mesh
nx, ny = mesh.node_x, mesh.node_y
fnc = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data
print("node_x:", nx.shape, " node_y:", ny.shape)
print("face_node_connectivity:", fnc.shape, " (n_face, max_vertices)")
fnc[:3]
    mesh = ds.mesh nx, ny = mesh.node_x, mesh.node_y fnc = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data print("node_x:", nx.shape, " node_y:", ny.shape) print("face_node_connectivity:", fnc.shape, " (n_face, max_vertices)") fnc[:3]
    node_x: (535,)  node_y: (535,)
face_node_connectivity: (724, 4)  (n_face, max_vertices)
    Out[8]:
    array([[ 0,  1,  2, -1],
       [ 3,  1,  0, -1],
       [ 1,  3,  4, -1]])

    face_areas gives the area of every face; face_centroids is a (2, n_face) array of face centre coordinates. Both are derived straight from the topology.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    areas = mesh.face_areas
cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids
print("face_areas:", areas.shape, " mean area:", round(float(areas.mean()), 4))
print("face_centroids:", (cx.shape, cy.shape))
    areas = mesh.face_areas cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids print("face_areas:", areas.shape, " mean area:", round(float(areas.mean()), 4)) print("face_centroids:", (cx.shape, cy.shape))
    face_areas: (724,)  mean area: 95242.3212
face_centroids: ((724,), (724,))

    Wireframe - the bare mesh¶

    plot_outline() draws the mesh edges with no data colouring. It is the fastest way to see the grid's shape, resolution, and how faces are distributed before looking at any results.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    _g = ds.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    _g = ds.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    Mapping the real results¶

    Surface elevation and the velocity components are time-varying (time_values lists the stored times, in seconds since the start). We pick a mid-simulation step with isel and map the tide level and the U-velocity.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    print("n timesteps:", len(ds.time_values))
step = ds.isel(time=6)  # a mid-run snapshot
    print("n timesteps:", len(ds.time_values)) step = ds.isel(time=6) # a mid-run snapshot
    n timesteps: 13
    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    _g = step.plot("Surface elevation", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Surface elevation (step 6)")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    _g = step.plot("Surface elevation", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Surface elevation (step 6)") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    _g = step.plot("Depth averaged U velocity", cmap="coolwarm", colorbar=True, title="Depth-averaged U velocity (step 6)")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    _g = step.plot("Depth averaged U velocity", cmap="coolwarm", colorbar=True, title="Depth-averaged U velocity (step 6)") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    From mesh to GIS¶

    A MeshDataset is not a dead end - it converts into the vector and raster types the rest of a GIS workflow expects. Everything below is reached through pyramids; this package only supplies the file-format driver that built the mesh.

    Faces as vector polygons¶

    to_geodataframe(variable_name=...) turns every face into a polygon row carrying that variable's value - a standard GeoPandas GeoDataFrame you can join, filter, or export.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    gdf = step.to_geodataframe(variable_name="Surface elevation")
print("rows:", len(gdf), " columns:", list(gdf.columns), " crs:", gdf.crs)
gdf.head()
    gdf = step.to_geodataframe(variable_name="Surface elevation") print("rows:", len(gdf), " columns:", list(gdf.columns), " crs:", gdf.crs) gdf.head()
    rows: 724  columns: ['Surface elevation', 'geometry']  crs: None

    Plotting that GeoDataFrame straight through GeoPandas (matplotlib under the hood) gives a choropleth of the same values, now as independent vector features.

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    ax = gdf.plot(column="Surface elevation", cmap="plasma", legend=True, figsize=(6, 5))
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Surface elevation - per-face polygons")
    ax = gdf.plot(column="Surface elevation", cmap="plasma", legend=True, figsize=(6, 5)) if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Surface elevation - per-face polygons")
    Out[15]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Surface elevation - per-face polygons')

    Dissolving into zones¶

    polygonize(variable) merges neighbouring faces that share a value into larger polygons - handy for turning a noisy per-cell field into clean zones. It needs a single value per face, which is exactly what our working dataset holds.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    zones = step.polygonize("Surface elevation")
print("dissolved polygons:", len(zones), " columns:", list(zones.columns))
ax = zones.plot(column="value", cmap="viridis", legend=True, figsize=(6, 5))
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Dissolved value zones")
    zones = step.polygonize("Surface elevation") print("dissolved polygons:", len(zones), " columns:", list(zones.columns)) ax = zones.plot(column="value", cmap="viridis", legend=True, figsize=(6, 5)) if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Dissolved value zones") 
    dissolved polygons: 724  columns: ['value', 'geometry']
    Out[16]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Dissolved value zones')

    Sampling at points¶

    sample(variable, x, y) reads the value of the face that contains each query point. Here we probe the first few face centroids, so each query lands squarely inside a face.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    cx, cy = ds.mesh.face_centroids
xs, ys = cx[:5], cy[:5]
vals = step.sample("Surface elevation", xs, ys)
for x, y, v in zip(xs, ys, vals):
    print(f"({x:10.2f}, {y:10.2f}) -> {float(v):.4f}")
    cx, cy = ds.mesh.face_centroids xs, ys = cx[:5], cy[:5] vals = step.sample("Surface elevation", xs, ys) for x, y, v in zip(xs, ys, vals): print(f"({x:10.2f}, {y:10.2f}) -> {float(v):.4f}")
    ( 222020.13, 6162900.67) -> -0.1208
( 221854.17, 6163191.33) -> -0.1204
( 221466.51, 6162980.50) -> -0.1205
( 219889.09, 6161480.17) -> -0.1302
( 220303.42, 6162214.50) -> -0.1160

    The mesh outline as one polygon¶

    bounding_polygon() returns a single shapely polygon tracing the mesh's outer boundary - the model's wetted footprint, useful as a clip mask or extent reference.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon()
import geopandas as gpd
ax = gpd.GeoSeries([poly]).plot(facecolor="none", edgecolor="crimson", figsize=(5, 5))
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Mesh bounding polygon")
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon() import geopandas as gpd ax = gpd.GeoSeries([poly]).plot(facecolor="none", edgecolor="crimson", figsize=(5, 5)) if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Mesh bounding polygon")
    Out[18]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Mesh bounding polygon')

    Cropping to a sub-region¶

    subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) returns a new, smaller MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box - the same object type, so every operation above still applies. We derive a box from the mesh envelope so it works on any extent.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = ds.bounds
mx, my = (xmin + xmax) / 2, (ymin + ymax) / 2
sub = ds.subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, mx, my)
print("faces in full mesh:", ds.n_face, " -> in subset:", sub.n_face)
_g = sub.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
plt.title("Lower-left quadrant subset")
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = ds.bounds mx, my = (xmin + xmax) / 2, (ymin + ymax) / 2 sub = ds.subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, mx, my) print("faces in full mesh:", ds.n_face, " -> in subset:", sub.n_face) _g = sub.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg) plt.title("Lower-left quadrant subset") 
    faces in full mesh: 724  -> in subset: 234
    Out[19]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Lower-left quadrant subset')

    Connectivity as a sparse graph¶

    sparse_adjacency() exposes face-to-face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix, and connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the mesh it belongs to - the entry points for graph algorithms over the grid.

    In [20]:
    Copied! 
    adj = ds.sparse_adjacency()
print("adjacency:", adj.shape, " non-zeros:", adj.nnz)
labels = ds.connected_components()
print("connected components:", len(np.unique(labels)))
    adj = ds.sparse_adjacency() print("adjacency:", adj.shape, " non-zeros:", adj.nnz) labels = ds.connected_components() print("connected components:", len(np.unique(labels)))
    adjacency: (724, 724)  non-zeros: 2248
connected components: 1

    Circumcenters - not applicable here¶

    circumcenters() is only defined for purely triangular meshes. This grid contains quad (or mixed-polygon) faces, so the call would raise ValueError. We note it and skip rather than force it.

    Self-contained rasterisation¶

    to_dataset(variable, cell_size=...) samples the mesh onto a regular raster grid and returns a pyramids Dataset. Unlike rasterize_like / regrid - which need an existing reference grid and are therefore skipped here - this is self-contained: you only choose a cell size.

    In [21]:
    Copied! 
    step_xy = (ds.bounds[2] - ds.bounds[0]) / 60
rast = step.to_dataset("Surface elevation", cell_size=step_xy)
print("rasterised to:", type(rast).__name__)
rast.plot()
plt.title("Surface elevation rasterised")
    step_xy = (ds.bounds[2] - ds.bounds[0]) / 60 rast = step.to_dataset("Surface elevation", cell_size=step_xy) print("rasterised to:", type(rast).__name__) rast.plot() plt.title("Surface elevation rasterised") 
    rasterised to: Dataset
    Out[21]:
    Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Surface elevation rasterised')

    Reprojection - skipped¶

    to_crs(...) needs a source CRS to project from. MIKE stores the projection in a side file, so ds.crs comes back None here even though the coordinates are UTM metres. With no source CRS, reprojection is undefined, so we skip it; assign a CRS first if your coordinates are georeferenced.

    Note — xarray interop. pyramids-core exposes a to_xarray() bridge to the xarray ecosystem, but these notebooks deliberately stay within pyramids-core's own GDAL-based UGRID I/O and do not use xarray. Its optional-dependency install hint is also currently broken upstream — tracked at serapeum-org/pyramids-core#1512.

    Takeaway¶

    DFSU brings DHI's flexible mesh into the same MeshDataset shape as every other driver. Its mixed triangle/quad topology rules out circumcenters(), but surface elevation and velocity map cleanly once a timestep is selected, and the vector/raster conversions behave identically. pyramids-mesh owns only the DFSU parsing; the analysis lives in pyramids.
